courses.title: UI Design: From Idea to Interface
courses.description: Build beautiful, useful interfaces with a process you can repeat.
requirements: A browser and time to practice

lessons.title: Understand the problem
lessons.content: Before opening a design tool, identify who you are designing for and the task they need to complete. Write a problem statement with a user, a need, and a reason. Interview questions should invite stories rather than suggest an answer.
lessons.exercise: Write a problem statement for a student trying to find the right course.

lessons.title: Build a visual hierarchy
lessons.content: Hierarchy tells people what to read first. Use scale, weight, spacing and contrast deliberately. Start with one primary action per section. Group related information with proximity and give separate groups breathing room.
lessons.exercise: Sketch a course card using three type sizes and one accent color.

lessons.title: Design accessible components
lessons.content: A reusable button needs default, hover, focus, disabled, and loading states. Visible labels and keyboard focus help everyone navigate. Do not rely only on color to communicate an error; add concise text.
lessons.exercise: List the states and labels for a course enrollment form.

lessons.title: Prototype, test, iterate
lessons.content: Test a small realistic task with a prototype. Observe where a participant hesitates before offering help. Record evidence separately from your interpretation. Prioritize changes by frequency and impact, then test again.
lessons.exercise: Ask a friend to locate a free beginner course in your sketch.

quiz.title: UI Design: From Idea to Interface · Knowledge check

questions.text: What should you define before visual design?
questions.explanation: Start with a user, their need, and the reason it matters.
Scale and spacing establish reading order.

questions.text: What should accompany an error color?
questions.explanation: Text ensures the error does not depend on color perception.

questions.text: A usability test is most useful when you…
options: Ask if the screen is pretty
questions.explanation: Observe real tasks to identify friction.

courses.title: Modern React, One Component at a Time
courses.description: Build a strong foundation in components, state and accessible interfaces.
requirements: A browser and time to practice

lessons.title: Think in components
lessons.content: A component describes part of a user interface. Start by splitting a page into responsibilities. A CourseCard can receive a title and price as props. Keeping data flow explicit makes components easier to reuse and test.
lessons.exercise: Break the Proerply dashboard into five components.

lessons.title: Props and local state
lessons.content: Props are inputs from a parent; local state is memory owned by a component. Use a state setter to update it. Derive values such as item counts from existing data instead of storing duplicate state.
lessons.exercise: Build a counter and derive a message from its count.

lessons.title: Render lists and forms
lessons.content: Use a stable item identifier as a key when rendering a list. Form controls need labels. Validate both client-side for feedback and server-side for trust. Keep pending and error states visible.
lessons.exercise: Create a filterable list with a labeled search input.

lessons.title: Effects and cleanup
lessons.content: An effect synchronizes with a system outside React, such as a timer or browser event. Return cleanup to remove subscriptions. Compute derived values while rendering when no external synchronization is needed.
lessons.exercise: Create a timer with cleanup when the component unmounts.

quiz.title: Modern React, One Component at a Time · Knowledge check

questions.explanation: Props carry explicit inputs into a component.
Stable keys preserve item identity.
Cleanup disconnects subscriptions and timers.

questions.text: Where must untrusted input be validated?
questions.explanation: Client checks improve UX; server checks enforce trust.

courses.title: Tell a Better Story with Data
courses.description: Turn a spreadsheet into a clear story and a better decision.
requirements: A browser and time to practice

lessons.title: Start with a question
lessons.content: A useful analysis starts with a decision and a question. Define the observation unit and the time period. Decide how missing values and duplicates affect your answer before drawing a chart.
lessons.exercise: Write an answerable question about course completion.

lessons.title: Clean with care
lessons.content: Inspect types, ranges, and missingness. A blank value is not always zero. Preserve the original dataset and record each transformation so another person can reproduce the analysis.
lessons.exercise: Describe how you would handle missing study times.

lessons.title: Choose the right chart
lessons.content: Use bars for comparing categories and lines for change over time. Label units and choose scales that represent differences honestly. A chart title can state the question or the main finding.
lessons.exercise: Sketch weekly lessons completed as a line chart.

lessons.title: Communicate uncertainty
lessons.content: An observed association is not necessarily causal. Note sample size, selection, and possible confounders. Present the most useful result with context, then propose the next measurement.
lessons.exercise: Write a short conclusion that includes one limitation.

quiz.title: Tell a Better Story with Data · Knowledge check

questions.text: What comes first in an analysis?
questions.explanation: The question guides the data and method.
Its meaning depends on collection and context.

questions.text: Which chart suits change over time?
questions.explanation: Lines show sequential trends clearly.
Confounding and study design matter.

courses.title: Everyday Photography, Extraordinary Stories
courses.description: Find better light, frame intentionally, and make everyday stories shine.
requirements: A browser and time to practice

lessons.title: Read the light
lessons.content: Notice the direction, softness, and color of light. A large window can be a soft light source. Move your subject relative to the light before changing camera settings.
lessons.exercise: Photograph one object near a window at two angles.

lessons.title: Compose with intention
lessons.content: Use edges and lines to direct attention. Check the background for distracting objects. Try a different camera height and distance rather than taking every photograph at eye level.
lessons.exercise: Make three compositions of the same subject.

lessons.title: Control exposure
lessons.content: Aperture, shutter time and sensitivity influence exposure. Fast shutter times reduce motion blur; longer exposures record movement. Change one variable at a time when learning.
lessons.exercise: Compare a moving subject with a fast and slow shutter.

lessons.title: Edit a visual story
lessons.content: Select images that serve a coherent story. Adjust exposure and color gently and keep the original files. A small sequence with a clear beginning, detail and conclusion is often stronger than many similar images.
lessons.exercise: Choose three photographs to describe your study space.

quiz.title: Everyday Photography, Extraordinary Stories · Knowledge check

questions.explanation: A larger apparent source produces gentler shadow transitions.

questions.text: What can improve a distracting composition?
questions.explanation: Moving can remove distracting overlaps.
Shorter exposure captures less movement.
Originals allow reversible edits.

courses.title: Build a Brand People Remember
courses.description: Connect strategy, voice and a consistent visual identity.
requirements: A browser and time to practice

lessons.title: Know your audience
lessons.content: A brand is a pattern of expectations and experiences. Define the audience and what they value. Study alternatives to understand where your offer can be meaningfully different.
lessons.exercise: Write one audience statement.

lessons.title: Define a point of view
lessons.content: A positioning statement connects an audience, a problem, a benefit and evidence. Avoid generic claims that every competitor can make. A specific promise is easier to communicate and deliver.
lessons.exercise: Draft a positioning statement for a learning studio.

lessons.title: Create a consistent system
lessons.content: Choose type, color and imagery that support the intended character. Record repeatable rules in a small guide. Consistency helps recognition, but each channel may need a different composition.
lessons.exercise: Write three visual guidelines.

lessons.title: Make the experience match
lessons.content: Promises only work when the product and support experience fulfill them. Review a complete customer journey and identify moments where your message and actual experience diverge.
lessons.exercise: Audit a welcome message and its first user action.

quiz.title: Build a Brand People Remember · Knowledge check

questions.explanation: Positioning starts with a defined audience and need.
Repeated patterns improve recognition.
The experience should deliver on the promise.
Guidelines make consistent application easier.

courses.title: Python for Curious Minds
courses.description: Practice small programs and solve useful everyday problems.
requirements: A browser and time to practice

lessons.title: Values and variables
lessons.content: Variables name values. Python has types such as integers, strings, lists and dictionaries. Use clear names that describe purpose and inspect unexpected values before adding complexity.
lessons.exercise: Create variables for a course title and lesson count.

lessons.title: Decisions and repetition
lessons.content: Use if statements to choose behavior and for loops to iterate over collections. Watch boundary conditions such as an empty list. Keep one loop focused on a clear task.
lessons.exercise: Count completed lessons in a list of booleans.

lessons.title: Small reusable functions
lessons.content: A function packages a useful behavior with explicit inputs and a result. Avoid hidden global state. Small functions with focused responsibilities are easier to test and reuse.
lessons.exercise: Write a function that computes a completion percentage.

lessons.title: Handle errors and files
lessons.content: Use a context manager when opening files. Catch specific exceptions when you can recover meaningfully. Report errors clearly instead of silently discarding them. Never execute untrusted code from input.
lessons.exercise: Describe how your program handles a missing input file.

quiz.title: Python for Curious Minds · Knowledge check

questions.explanation: Dictionaries associate keys with values.
It repeats work for each item.
Clear boundaries improve reuse and tests.
Context managers close resources reliably.
